message.reasoning:
I'm ready to play Monopoly.

I own a dark blue monopoly and can build one house for $200. I'll place it evenly across Park Place and Boardwalk.

One house would raise rent to $200 on Boardwalk and $175 on Park Place. But that leaves only $63 cash, which is too risky. I'll skip building for now.

No opponent has a monopoly yet, so rent is low. The risk of bankruptcy is minimal, making the $200 house investment safer than first thought.

Dark blue is only two spaces out of forty, so landing there is unlikely. The $63 cash reserve is too thin to justify the house cost.

Mortgaging other properties could free up cash, but that would break the dark blue monopoly. Six houses on each property would cost $1200, which is impossible with current funds.

Mortgaging St. Charles, Water Works, and Penn RR would raise cash to $408, enough for two houses with only $8 left over. That is still too risky. The even-building rule allows a one-house difference, so one house on each property is the safer path.

Opponents have far more cash than I do. p1 has $584, p3 has $873, and p4 has $985. They will try to complete monopolies through trades. p3 already owns orange properties and wants reds, but the red monopoly is split three ways. I need to watch for trade threats.

I am the only player with a completed monopoly. This is a huge advantage. I should build houses immediately to start charging high rents before opponents assemble their sets.

p1 owns States, Indiana, Pennsylvania Ave, and B&O. p4 owns Mediterranean, Electric Company, New York, and North Carolina. Neither has a full set yet.

Oriental is owned by p3. Vermont and Connecticut are unowned. p3 may buy them. Atlantic, Ventnor, and Marvin Gardens are all unowned.

The board is wide open. My monopoly is the only one. Building houses now starts the clock on bankrupting others when they land on dark blue.

Risk of $63 cash: 
- Income tax/luxury tax if I land: luxury tax $75, income tax $200. I couldn't pay luxury tax ($75) with $63 without mortgaging.
- But I just ended my movement (I'm on Boardwalk, post-turn). Next turn I'll roll from Boardwalk. Possible lands: GO (collect $200!), or Mediterranean through Chance etc.

Boardwalk is near GO. The next roll lands on cheap or unowned spaces, so the $63 cash reserve is safe for one turn. I am reconsidering whether to build a house on Boardwalk.

Boardwalk is hit roughly 2.5% of the time, so the $200 house would need two successful hits to break even. The real value is signaling strength and building toward three houses, which is the peak ROI. I should raise cash before building more.

Mortgaging non-monopoly properties could free up cash for houses. Kentucky, St. Charles, Penn RR, and Water Works are all poor choices. Their unimproved rent is too low to justify the mortgage value.

Mortgaging all four non-monopoly properties would raise cash to $618, enough for three houses with $18 left over. Placing two houses on Boardwalk and one on Park Place would cost $600. Boardwalk rent would jump to $600, which is devastating against p1's $584 balance.

A $600 house would hurt every opponent, but $18 cash is too risky. I already mortgaged everything else, so bankruptcy would lose the entire dark blue monopoly. I need a safe cash buffer and must avoid building houses right now.

The highest possible rent from a single hit is only about $28 on Pennsylvania Avenue. p4's utility could reach $48, but that is rare. The immediate danger of bankruptcy is far lower than assumed.

Chance and Community Chest cards can demand $50 or $150. With only $18 cash, that would force bankruptcy. Mortgaging everything to build three houses is therefore suicidal. I will build just one house and keep the full $63 cash reserve.

I will keep mortgage capacity available for future debts. One house on Park Place raises rent by $105, while one on Boardwalk raises it by $100. I will build one house on Boardwalk now.

Boardwalk's first house raises absolute rent to $200, while Park Place's first house raises it to $175. Park Place offers slightly better incremental rent for the initial investment. Boardwalk's later houses scale harder, but for a single house the return is marginally lower.

Boardwalk is the better choice for a single house because its $200 absolute rent can deal more damage than Park Place's $175. Even mortgaging St. Charles for $70 would only raise cash to $333, which still covers just one house and leaves $133.

Mortgaging Kentucky alone would raise cash to $373, still only enough for one house. Two houses require $400, so I need roughly $137 more. Combining St. Charles and Water Works yields $145, but that leaves just $8 after building two houses. Mortgaging Kentucky and St. Charles raises cash to $443, allowing two houses with $43 left over while keeping the utility blocker and railroad income intact. Mortgaging Penn RR and Kentucky would leave $73 after building two houses, though it sacrifices both the railroad rent and Kentucky's rent.

Mortgaging Kentucky and St. Charles for two houses leaves $43 cash, plus Penn RR and Water Works as a $175 emergency buffer against chance cards. This is the right play. Only one action per turn is allowed.

I must mortgage before building to raise cash first. Building then mortgaging would leave only one house. Water Works is the top priority to keep because it blocks p4's utility monopoly.

Mortgaging Water Works still blocks p4's utility pair because mortgaged properties can still be traded. The rent loss is minor. Kentucky is the best mortgage target for cash, while St. Charles offers little value.

Mortgaging Kentucky and Penn RR raises cash to $473. Two houses cost $400, leaving a $73 buffer. The unmortgaged St. Charles and Water Works still collect rent as blockers. Emergency mortgage capacity totals $218. Building three houses would leave only $18 with no emergency buffer, so that path is rejected.

I am reconsidering whether to build houses this turn. Trading could raise cash or complete another monopoly, but the risks are high. p3 might pay a large sum for Kentucky to finish the red set, yet that would create a competing monopoly if they also acquire Indiana from p1. p1 might want St. Charles to complete the pink set and then buy Virginia, which is dangerous. p4 might want Water Works to complete utilities.

Water Works is a weak utility. p4 has $985 and might pay $200–300 for it, but they seem conservative. Trading blockers to fund dark blue houses is risky because p3 has $873 and could build red houses immediately.

Red and orange properties are landed on more frequently than dark blue, so a red monopoly with houses is the better investment. I will keep Kentucky, St. Charles, and Water Works as blockers rather than selling them. I am also considering trading Penn RR to p1 for cash; that would give them two railroads, but that is not game-breaking.

I will not sell Penn RR to p1. Unmortgaging costs 10% interest, so the $121 cost to restore Kentucky is acceptable if the houses generate enough rent. I am still deciding whether to mortgage Kentucky first or simply build one house with my current cash.

I will mortgage Kentucky Avenue and Pennsylvania Railroad. Water Works and St. Charles Place will stay unmortgaged as blockers and emergency funds. I am deciding whether to send a public message about raising cash for dark blue houses, or remain silent to avoid provoking trades.

A calm public message about needing liquidity is preferable to a threatening one. I am also weighing whether to buy unowned properties instead of building houses, since p3 might race for the light blue monopoly.

All yellow properties are unowned. Atlantic, Ventnor, and Marvin cost $260 to $280 each. I can afford one if I land there. That would give me a second monopoly path. I am on Boardwalk.

I will not land on the yellows next turn. From Boardwalk I must roll 8 or 9 to reach Vermont and Connecticut, which are light blue properties. I am mapping the exact spaces for the next roll.

Rolling 5 from Boardwalk lands on Income Tax. With only $63 cash, paying the $200 tax would force bankruptcy unless I mortgage something first.

I will assume the engine allows mortgaging to pay debts, since the action state includes mortgage as a post-turn option. I should keep enough cash to cover the $200 income tax or have a clear mortgage plan ready.

Keeping $263 cash is more valuable than building a house. The next roll could land on Baltic ($60), Reading RR ($200), Vermont ($100), or Connecticut ($120). With $263, I can buy any of those properties and still retain $63. Building a house now would waste that liquidity.

Mortgaging to build two houses would leave no cash for Reading RR or the light blues. I cannot complete the light blue monopoly without trading for Oriental, and p3 will not sell it.

Blocking p3's light blue monopoly is valuable, but buying those properties now is risky. Purchase decisions happen on landing, and mortgaging to pay for them may not be possible at that moment. I will keep $263 liquid for now.

Delaying house construction by one turn risks opponents landing on the undeveloped dark blue properties and paying only $70 or $100 in rent instead of the full $175 or $200. Three other players will roll before I can act again, so the probability of that happening is significant.

The expected value of one house over three opponent turns is only about fifteen dollars. Reading Railroad and light blue blockers are worth far more than that.

The first house on Boardwalk would yield only about seven dollars per round in expected rent, meaning a payback period of roughly twenty-seven rounds. That is far too slow to justify building now.

Three houses on Boardwalk would yield $1400 per hit, while one house only pays back about seven dollars per round. The real target is the kill shot of three houses on both dark blue properties, not a single house. Building now would deplete cash and prevent reaching that threshold.

Two houses on Boardwalk would yield $600 in rent, which is enough to bankrupt p1. That is why the optimal play is to wait and not build yet.

I will wait to accumulate a $600 buffer before building. That may take four to six orbits, and opponents could complete monopolies in the meantime. The unowned yellows are especially dangerous because they are high-traffic and expensive to develop.

p3 can build three houses on the light blue set for only $150. That yields $270–$300 in rent per hit, which is far faster than the dark blue houses.

No color group is fully monopolized yet. The orange, green, pink, and red sets are split across players. p4 could complete the brown set by buying Baltic from me, since they already own Med. Brown houses cost only $50 each and hotels pay $250–$450, so that path is cheap to develop.

I will not reach the unowned yellows for about one and a half to two turns, so I need cash on hand to buy them. Atlantic, Ventnor, and Marvin each cost roughly $260 to $280.

I will end this turn without building or mortgaging. Keeping $263 liquid lets me buy a yellow property if I land there, starting a monopoly race on the best available unowned set. The dark blue rent is already doubled.

I am evaluating trade proposals to improve my position. Acquiring the red set from p1 and p3 would require impossible demands, so that path is closed. I am now considering offering Water Works to p4 for cash, which would complete their utilities.

I will not propose trades. Selling Water Works for cash would cost too much, and p3 will not give up Illinois cheaply. I will end this turn without building or mortgaging.

messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.
